newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Islamists take anti-Bhutto campaign to streets.
newsitem.headline: Islamists take anti-Bhutto campaign to streets.

text.p: A trial of strength between Pakistan's Islamic militants and Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's security forces crippled normal life in Islamabad on Sunday.
Police used tear gas and batons in running skirmishes with stone-throwing protesters trying to burst a security cordon clamped around the Pakistani capital. About 29 people were hurt.
The attempt to bring "one million" supporters into the capital for a sit-in outside parliament was a typical ploy by the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party led by Qazi Hussain Ahmad.
JI, with a strong base in student politics, has long shown more skill at mobilising its youthful adherents for battles with police than for winning votes in Pakistan's fragile democracy.

The party, which has a long history of bitter rivalry with Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP), won just three seats in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) at the last general election in October 1993, which brought Bhutto to power.
Together all the Islamist parties won only nine seats, down from the 17 they had gained at the previous election in 1990.
All three JI members of parliament resigned their seats on Saturday, following the example of Ahmad, who quit his Senate seat last month as part of his campaign to topple Bhutto.
While it has never enjoyed much success at the polls, the JI and other Islamist parties, equally poor at vote-getting, exert a political influence disproportionate to their popularity.
JI was founded in 1942 by the influential religious thinker Maulana Abul Ala Maududi, who opposed the creation of Pakistan, partitioned from India in 1947. He died in 1979.
Maududi, revered by the Egyptian-based Moslem Brotherhood organisation, held that jihad, or holy war, could be waged against all forces threatening Islam at home or abroad.

JI swung to prominence in the 1970s when it fiercely opposed Bhutto's secularist father, then prime minister Zulfikar Ali, and used its power to force him to ban alcohol and move Pakistan's weekly holiday to Friday from Sunday.
No Pakistani government since has felt strong enough to reverse those moves by Bhutto to curry favour with the mullahs (Moslem clerics).

Nevertheless, the Sunni Moslem Jamaat-i-Islami has never been able to build an effective mass movement by fusing the economic grievances and religious sentiments of Pakistan's 130 million people, about four-fifths of whom are Sunnis.
"Revolution, revolution, Islamic revolution," chanted JI supporters as they faced police in riot gear on Sunday.

But the secular PPP and main opposition Pakistan Muslim League led by Nawaz Sharif still dominate Pakistani politics, however disenchanted ordinary people have become with what many see as poor governance, corruption and economic burdens.
The two main parties have kept their grip on power largely due to Pakistan's formidable landowners, who virtually control the votes of the peasantry working their lands.
The religious parties have also dissipated their energies in sectarian quarrels between Sunni and Shi'ite Moslems, as well as in support for external causes such as Kashmir and Afghanistan.
JI sponsors Hizb-ul-Mujahideen, one of the Kashmiri factions in the separatist revolt against Indian rule since 1990.
It also played a role in supporting Afghan mujahideen guerrilla factions fighting the Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
But JI has relatively few links with Afghanistan's fundamentalist Taleban movement that captured Kabul a month ago.
Many leaders of the Taleban, or religious students, attended Islamic schools run for Afghan refugees in Pakistan by the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam of Maulana Fazl-ur-Rahman, a PPP ally.
Ahmad, 58, the JI's leader, is the son of a mullah from the town of Ziarat Sahib Kaka Khail in the religiously conservative North West Frontier Province.

An activist with Jamaat-i-Islami's student wing, he later lectured at Peshawar University before starting a business career. He became secretary-general of the party in 1978 and was first elected as its Amir (prince) in 1987.
Ahmad won a Senate seat in 1986 and was elected to a second six-year term in 1992.
